title: Towards quantum machine learning for assessing the resilience of post-quantum cryptography
abstract: The potential capabilities of quantum computers motivated the development of cryptographic protocols suitable for securing communication against adversaries with access to large fault-tolerant quantum computers. However, even though current quantum computers are limited in terms of size and precision, they can still be useful for finding loopholes and weaknesses in the post-quantum cryptographic protocols. In this work, we present an attempt to utilize the capabilities of Quantum Generative Adversarial Networks (QGANs), one of the promising architectures used in quantum machine learning, for this purpose. We describe an example application of QGAN architecture for the purpose of loading the probability distribution of the hash-based digital signatures into the memory of a quantum computer. Our results confirm that near-term hybrid quantum-classical methods possess capabilities required for this purpose. The presented approach can be used as a first step in the workflow, enabling the utilization of quantum computing for attacking post-quantum cryptographic primitives.
summary: This paper proposes using Quantum Generative Adversarial Networks (QGANs) as a tool to test the security of Post-Quantum Cryptography. By training QGANs on cryptographic signature data, the authors demonstrate that near-term quantum hardware can learn these complex probability distributions. This suggests a viable pathway for utilizing quantum computation in cryptanalysis workflows.
main_problem: The primary goal is assessing the resilience of Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) protocols against potential attacks leveraging quantum computational capabilities.
main_result: The study confirms that near-term hybrid quantum-classical methods, specifically using QGANs, possess sufficient capability to learn and approximate the complex probability distributions underlying PQC signatures.
method: A Quantum Generative Adversarial Network (QGAN) framework is employed. The generator prepares a quantum state representing the data distribution, while a classical discriminator network attempts to distinguish between real and generated samples.
model_or_system: The model utilizes QGANs, which are hybrid quantum-classical architectures. The core task involves loading the probability distribution of hash-based digital signatures (like SPHINCS+) into a quantum state $|\psi_tangle$.
key_observables: Kullback-Leibler divergence ($D_{KL}(P \parallel Q)$) is used to quantify the approximation quality between the true and generated distributions.
important_parameters: The number of qubits ($n$), the structure/number of parameters in the quantum ansatz (e.g., N-local, real-amplitudes), and training loss metrics are key parameters.
main_assumptions: The approach is limited by current Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) technology; the results are based on simulation and do not constitute a full cryptanalytic attack.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the QGAN architecture, show sample data from PQC signatures, track training loss over epochs, and compare $D_{KL}$ divergence across different quantum ansatz types for both real and simple distributions.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of PQC security assessment using quantum methods. It details the QGAN methodology, applies it to SPHINCS+ signatures, compares various quantum circuit ansatze (N-local vs. real-amplitudes), analyzes convergence via loss functions, and concludes with the potential implications for cryptanalysis.
why_interesting: While focused on cryptography, the underlying mechanism—using variational quantum circuits to model complex probability distributions—is highly relevant to simulating many-body quantum states or learning Hamiltonians in condensed matter physics.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Architecture of the proposed framework based on hybrid quantum-classical QGAN from the Qiskit Machine Learning library [4, 36]. The quantum generator is trained using the feedback from the classical discriminator to generate a quantum state suitable for representing the observed real data. Details of the quantum circuit construction are described in Section 3.3. Details of the classical discriminator are described in Fig. 3.

Fig. 2. Three types of ansatze used in this work as the basic blocks of the quantum generator. The circuits in this figure were built for four-qubit registers. We have (a) six, (b) eight, and (c) sixteen trainable parameters per layer. Using (a) and (c) we do not impose restrictions on the form of generated quantum states. For the case (b) the prepared quantum states will only have real amplitudes.
Fig. 3. Architecture of the artificial neural network used as the discriminator in the presented method. The scheme is based on the implementation described in [4,36].

Fig. 4. Sample data from (a) the post-quantum hash-based source and (b) an artificially created mixture of multivariate normal distributions. (a) Probability distribution of pairs of four-bit words generated from the first byte of the SPHINCS+ signatures. A sample obtained using 213 signatures for a single plain text. (b) Probability distribution obtained as a mixture of 16 multivariate normal distributions, with parameters adjusted to (0, 15) × (0, 15) grid.
Fig. 5. Value of the loss function for the generator and the discriminator during the learning process for the PQC data.
